newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Slovak rates up on liquidity crunch, seen steady.
newsitem.headline: Slovak rates up on liquidity crunch, seen steady.

text.p: Slovak interbank money market rates soared on Wednesday due to a shortage of market liquidity with dealers saying they did not expect rates to recede in the coming days.
Traders said the jump was the result of central bank (NBS) efforts to keep the market short of liquidity to bolster the Slovak crown.

"The NBS seems to be deliberately keeping the market short of liquidity as it wants to prevent a similar critical situation such as the one which occurred in the Czech Republic," said Martin Hrozany of Credit Lyonnais.

Slovak rates up to two weeks rose to above 30 percent on Wednesday, after opening at below 20 percent, as the banking sector lacked some four billion crowns to meet minimum reserve requirements later this month.
The Czech crown has been under strong downward pressure since the end of last week, prompting the Czech National Bank (CNB) to intervene on the market to support the currency.

The CNB intensified its battle to shore up the weary crown on Wednesday, imposing further limits on banks' access to the last resort lending facility, the Lombard rate, and thus limiting access to crown funds which could be converted to hard currencies.
"This jump in (Slovak rates) is due to fears on the market that something like the Czech turmoil could happen also here," said Rasto Zivor, a trader at ING Bank.
Zivor did not expect rates to ease in the near future as he said the NBS seemed to be satisfied with the current liquidity shortage.

"But, on the other hand, we do not think rates will go significantly higher, let's say to above 36 percent, as their high levels can again attract liquidity from abroad, playing on the interest rate differential," he added.
Short-term funds on the Prague interbank money market were trading at record levels of over 100 percent on Wednesday as CNB measures brought acute liquidity shortage.
"Some local banks fear this could happen also in Slovakia and that is why they are closing their short crown positions to meet the minimum reserve demand with cheaper funds," Zivor said.
